findings.issue_text: [BUG] `backupCode` was added to `LoginValues` and registered via `methods.register("backupCode")` in BackupCode.tsx, but the zod `formSchema` that `zodResolver(formSchema)` enforces on this form was not updated to include a `backupCode` key, so zod strips the unknown field from the validated values passed to submit. When a user clicks 'Lost access' and submits a backup code, `signIn("credentials", ...)` is called without `backupCode`, so `authorize` takes the `totpCode` branch and throws `SecondFactorRequired`; the lost-access login flow can never succeed even with a valid code.

[ADVISORY] The new file's default export is declared as `export default function TwoFactor({ center = true })` inside BackupCode.tsx, duplicating the name of the sibling TwoFactor.tsx component. Anyone importing, stack-tracing, or React DevTools-inspecting this component sees two distinct components both named `TwoFactor`; the next change to either file (e.g. hoisting shared logic or adding a displayName-based test selector) becomes ambiguous, and import collisions are one refactor away.

[ADVISORY] The download control nests a `<Button>` (which renders a `<button>` element) inside an `<a>` anchor, which is invalid interactive-content nesting. Clicking the inner button in some browsers/assistive tech triggers inconsistent behavior (the anchor's `download` navigation may be swallowed or double-activated), and the keyboard focus order exposes two competing interactive elements to screen-reader users on the backup-codes step.

[ADVISORY] Backup codes are generated and persisted to the user row in the `setup` endpoint (the password-confirmation step), before the user has actually enabled 2FA or even seen the codes. A user who opens the enable dialog, confirms their password, then cancels has silently had any previously issued backup codes overwritten (or new ones created) without ever viewing them — and since the login/disable paths reject a backupCode attempt only after password validation, a user who later 'loses access' and tries a code they saved from an earlier setup attempt gets `IncorrectBackupCode` with no hint that their stored list is stale.

[BUG] The login form's zod schema (formSchema, used via zodResolver on the same useForm that registers backupCode) is not updated for the new backupCode field, so zodResolver strips the unknown key and credentials.backupCode is undefined when passed to the credentials provider, making the backup-code login path in next-auth-options.ts unreachable from the login page. Users who click 'Lost access' and enter a valid backup code still get SecondFactorRequired / never authenticate via backup code on the login page, because the submitted values are parsed through the untouched zod schema before reaching signIn.

[ADVISORY] The diff's own TODO ('add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup') confirms the two new backend branches — the backupCode branch in next-auth-options.ts authorize() and the backupCode branch in disable.ts — plus the single-use consumption logic (backupCodes[index] = null and re-encrypt) have zero test coverage in this diff. A regression in the backup-code verification, single-use consumption, or wipe-on-disable logic ships silently; the e2e suite only exercises code display/download/copy, so a broken backup-code login is discovered by locked-out end users.

[ADVISORY] Backup-code verification and consumption are not atomic: two concurrent sign-in attempts with the same code both pass the indexOf check before either request reaches the user.update that nulls the code, so a backup code is replayable within that window. An attacker who briefly obtains a code (e.g. from a screenshot or leaked download) can reuse it concurrently with the legitimate user; single-use semantics ('Each backup code can be used exactly once') are violated.

[ADVISORY] The backup-code comparison is case-sensitive against lowercase hex (crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")), while the input placeholder 'XXXXX-XXXXX' suggests uppercase entry and the UI does no normalization beyond dash removal. A user typing a code in uppercase (natural given the placeholder) gets 'Backup code is incorrect' despite entering the correct code; they burn attempts and conclude their codes are wrong.

[ADVISORY] When CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY is missing, the disable endpoint throws new Error(ErrorCode.InternalServerError) instead of returning res.status(500).json({error: ...}) like every sibling branch in the same handler, so the client's response.json() in DisableTwoFactorModal throws and the user sees no error message. Operators who deploy without the encryption key get an unhandled 500 (uncaught in the handler) and the modal hangs in the catch-branch or shows nothing, instead of the handled 'something went wrong' message; next-auth's parallel code path has the same throw-instead-of-return pattern.

[ADVISORY] Backup codes are generated, persisted, and returned in plaintext in the setup response before the user has confirmed anything, and a user who abandons the flow after step one ends up with stored backupCodes the user has never seen (they were never displayed since DisplayBackupCodes only runs after enable), while the enable endpoint (totp/enable.ts, untouched by this diff) has no sanity check that backupCodes still match the setup that produced the displayed QR code. A user who starts setup, sees the QR code, but closes and later re-runs setup before enabling ends up displaying/enabling against a fresh secret while stale-looking backup codes from an intermediate setup run may have been shown or downloaded — the codes shown at DisplayBackupCodes step come from the first setup response held in component state, which is correct, but a dialog closed via onOpenChange (X button) does not run resetState, so reopening the modal resumes at the stale DisplayBackupCodes step with codes from the prior user's session state rendered again.

[ADVISORY] The 'missing_backup_codes' user-facing message ("Please generate them in your settings") promises a settings path to regenerate backup codes, but this diff ships no UI, API endpoint, or settings section that can regenerate or re-display backup codes after initial enablement. A user who lost their codes (or skipped the DisplayBackupCodes screen) hits a dead end: the error text instructs them to do something the product cannot do; support tickets and locked-out accounts follow.

[BUG] Backup codes are generated and persisted during the setup step, before 2FA is ever confirmed, and the only place they are shown to the user is after successful enable — a user who runs setup and abandons the flow (or closes the modal at the QR/TOTP step) has 10 valid, never-revealed backup codes silently stored against their account. Users who enabled 2FA via any earlier path or who abandoned setup have stored backup codes they never saw and cannot view again; the single-use consumption in login then deletes codes the user never knew existed, and the codes were accepted as valid second factors without ever being delivered.

[BUG] At SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes the footer omits the cancel/reset wiring that other steps have, and the Dialog's onOpenChange path (ESC / outside click) neither calls resetState() nor onEnable(), so the parent component's 2FA state is never updated when the dialog is dismissed that way. A user who dismisses the backup-codes step with ESC sees the settings toggle still read 'disabled' even though 2FA is fully enabled server-side; the UI and server state diverge until a page refresh.

[ADVISORY] The single-use consumption logic (index lookup, null-out, re-encrypt, prisma update) that backs the core 'each backup code can be used exactly once' invariant has no test anywhere in this diff — the only related test is a TODO comment in login.2fa.e2e.ts line 12. A regression in code consumption (e.g. failing to null the used code, or re-encrypting the unmodified array) would allow unlimited reuse of one backup code — precisely the invariant the feature claims — and CI would stay green.

[ADVISORY] The tabIndex={-1} change to PasswordField's visibility toggle is not traceable to the 2FA backup-code requirement and is an unrelated behavioral change bundled into this PR. Keyboard users across every password field in the app lose the ability to tab to the show/hide password toggle; the change ships unannounced inside a feature PR, so the accessibility regression is easy to miss in review.

[ADVISORY] The object URL created for the backup-codes download (URL.createObjectURL) is revoked only when a new setup run replaces it, never when the modal unmounts, and resetState() does not clear it. Each open/abandon cycle of the setup modal leaks a Blob URL holding the user's live backup codes in memory for the page's lifetime; long-lived sessions accumulate the leak.

[ADVISORY] setup.ts calls symmetricEncrypt with process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY without the presence guard that the login and disable handlers added in this same diff, so the new backupCodes write path throws an unhandled TypeError when the key is unset rather than returning a structured error. Operators running without CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY get a raw 500 from /setup with no console.error breadcrumb, inconsistent with the sibling handlers that handle the same condition explicitly in this PR.

[ADVISORY] The disable handler throws new Error(ErrorCode.InternalServerError) on a missing encryption key instead of returning a JSON error response like every other branch in the same handler. The client's response.json() in DisableTwoFactorModal parses an HTML 500 error page and throws, surfacing 'something went wrong' via the catch path instead of a clean InternalServerError message shown to the user.

[BUG] Backup-code consumption in authorize() is a non-atomic read-modify-write: JSON.parse of the stored blob, indexOf, then a separate prisma.user.update, with no conditional WHERE on the code still being present. Two concurrent logins submitting the same backup code both pass the indexOf check (both read the pre-update blob) and both are granted a session while only one consumption is persisted — a one-time code authenticates twice; the fix requires an atomic guarded update or hashed per-code rows with a uniqueness constraint.

[BUG] The 'no codes' sentinel is unrepresentable: MissingBackupCodes is only raised when the backupCodes column is null, but consumption writes JSON arrays of null entries, so a user who has burned all 10 codes has a non-null column of nulls. A user with zero remaining codes gets 'Backup code is incorrect' on every attempt instead of the 'missing_backup_codes' guidance ('generate them in your settings'), permanently and misleadingly — the same check exists in disable.ts and fails identically there.

[ADVISORY] The setup endpoint regenerates and persists a fresh backupCodes set on every invocation, and the only place the codes are ever displayed to the user is the final DisplayBackupCodes step of the enable flow. A user who confirms their password (triggering setup) and then cancels at the QR/TOTP steps has their previously-issued backup codes silently invalidated with no notice; they will later hit 'Backup code is incorrect'/'missing backup codes' with codes they carefully saved. The user-facing consequence appears at next-auth-options.ts:131.

[ADVISORY] Backup codes are stored reversibly encrypted (symmetricEncrypt of the plaintext codes) in a single TEXT JSON column instead of one-way hashed per-code rows, unlike one-time-code best practice. Anyone with DB read access plus the CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY (a single shared secret, no rotation) recovers all valid unused codes for every user; hashed per-code rows in a child table would also fix the consumption atomicity and the null-array sentinel problems in one shape change.

[ADVISORY] The disable endpoint's contract now accepts both code and backupCode in one payload, and the server branch prefers backupCode whenever it is truthy, so the discrimination between 'TOTP path' and 'backup path' lives in field-emptiness rather than an explicit factor type. Any future form change that leaves a stale backupCode value in the form (e.g. a variant of resetForm that preserves it) silently routes disable through the backup-code branch and returns IncorrectBackupCode for a user who typed a valid TOTP code; the login page has the same implicit precedence in next-auth-options.ts:131, and the two client copies (Login form, DisableTwoFactorModal) of this dual-field convention will drift.

[BUG] The onEnable callback contract was silently changed: onEnable() now fires only when the user clicks the backup-codes 'Close' button, not when 2FA is actually enabled. If the user dismisses the dialog via the Dialog's own close affordance (X button, Escape, or onOpenChange path), 2FA is enabled server-side but the parent's onEnable handler never runs — the settings switch keeps showing 2FA as disabled while the account is actually protected, so the user believes 2FA is off and the UI shows a state that contradicts the server.

[BUG] resetState() is only invoked from the Cancel button and the backup-codes Close button, never from the Dialog's onOpenChange, so closing via Escape/X leaves the component's step state at DisplayBackupCodes. The next time the user opens the enable-2FA dialog they land directly on the 'Backup Codes' step showing the previous session's codes, skipping the password and QR/TOTP steps entirely and displaying codes that may already be stale — the enable flow's intended starting state is silently replaced by leftover state.

[BUG] Every call to the setup endpoint regenerates and overwrites the stored backupCodes, invalidating any codes previously issued and saved by the user. A user who runs the enable flow (or re-runs setup after a failed attempt) gets a new batch of codes each time; any codes they already downloaded/copied in a prior setup call are silently dead, directly contradicting the user-facing copy 'Each backup code can be used exactly once' and the backup-code recovery promise.

[BUG] tabIndex={-1} is added unconditionally to the shared PasswordField visibility-toggle button, removing it from keyboard tab order in every password field across the entire app. Keyboard-only and screen-reader users of all existing PasswordFields (login, DisableTwoFactorModal, etc.) can no longer reach the show/hide password toggle via Tab, an accessibility regression smuggled into a 2FA feature PR and affecting surfaces far outside the PR's stated intent.

[ADVISORY] The new BackupCode component's default export is still named `TwoFactor`, copy-pasted from the component it was cloned from. Anyone debugging a stack trace, React DevTools entry, or import site sees two distinct components both reporting the name 'TwoFactor', making future changes to backup-code behavior harder to trace and increasing the risk of editing the wrong file.

[ADVISORY] The disable endpoint's backup-code branch accepts a backup code without consuming it (relies on the later blanket `backupCodes: null` clear), and the branch ordering means a valid backup code bypasses the TOTP check entirely while `req.body.code` is ignored. This is internally consistent for disable (codes are wiped anyway), but the asymmetry with the login path (which does consume per-code) is undocumented behavior that a future maintainer adding partial disable or backup-code reuse will trip over; the e2e TODO at apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts:12 confirms disable-with-backup-code is untested, so a regression here ships silently.

[BUG] Backup code consumption uses a read-decrypt-modify-encrypt-write sequence with no transaction or conditional update, so the same backup code can be replayed in concurrent requests. Two simultaneous logins submitting the same backup code both pass the indexOf check before either write lands (next-auth credentials callbacks run concurrently), so a single one-time code grants two sessions — defeating the single-use guarantee the copy promises ('Each backup code can be used exactly once') and letting an attacker who sniffed/copied a code use it even after the legitimate user already consumed it, if requests race.

[ADVISORY] Backup codes are generated with crypto.randomBytes(5).toString('hex'), yielding only 40 bits of entropy per code, well below the conventional 80+ bits for backup/recovery codes. An attacker who can submit many login attempts (e.g. via the credentials endpoint where rate limiting is per-IP and trivially distributed) has a materially better chance of guessing a valid code than against an 80-bit code; users with weak/leaked passwords get a second factor that is meaningfully brute-forceable.

[ADVISORY] Backup code verification uses backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode...) — a plain, early-exiting string comparison rather than a constant-time comparison (timingEqual/crypto.timingSafeEqual), and the same non-constant-time indexOf appears in disable.ts. Each failed attempt leaks how many leading characters of a candidate code match positions in the stored list (indexOf short-circuits per element, === per character); combined with the 40-bit code size this measurably aids online guessing by an automated attacker. Rebuttal: per-request timing jitter makes the leak impractical — but with 10 ordered codes and 40-bit values the leak compounds across attempts rather than being neutralized.

[ADVISORY] Every call to /setup regenerates and overwrites the stored backupCodes, silently invalidating any codes the user previously saved. A user who re-runs setup (re-scanning the QR into a new device, or any client that calls the setup endpoint) permanently voids the backup codes they already printed/stored, and they will only discover this during account recovery when every saved code returns IncorrectBackupCode — the exact lost-access scenario backup codes exist to prevent.

[ADVISORY] The missing-encryption-key branch throws new Error(ErrorCode.InternalServerError) instead of returning a res.status(500).json({error: ...}) like every other error path in the handler. An operator who misconfigures CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY gets an unhandled exception (stack trace in server logs, generic 500 HTML to the client) instead of a structured error the frontend's errorMessages map can render, turning a config problem into an opaque crash for the user disabling 2FA.

[ADVISORY] The disable endpoint accepts a backup code without deleting the used code from the list before success, relying entirely on the final backupCodes: null write at line 107 — and it checks the code against a list that may contain nulls from prior logins but performs no audit/logging of backup-code-based 2FA disable. Two concurrent disable requests both pass the indexOf check and both proceed (same race as the login path), and an attacker who obtains password + one backup code can disable 2FA with no security event logged for monitoring/alerting that a recovery-code-based disable occurred.

[BUG] The 2FA-enable e2e test uses `expect(...isChecked()).toBeTruthy()`, a false-confidence assertion that passes even when the switch is not checked, as the diff's own FIXME comment admits. The enable-2FA flow's core success state (the toggle actually switching on) is unverified; a regression that renders the switch unchecked while still returning 200 from setup/enable passes this test, and every downstream 2FA test in the file inherits the false confidence.

[BUG] The backup-code login branch in authorize() — including the one-time-use consumption logic (`backupCodes[index] = null` + re-encrypt) and the IncorrectBackupCode/MissingBackupCodes error paths — has zero test coverage in this diff; I checked apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts (the only test file changed), which exercises only the TOTP enable/download/copy path. The single-use invariant of backup codes is completely unverified: a bug that reuses a burned code, fails to persist the null, or throws the wrong ErrorCode ships silently, allowing replayed backup codes to grant account access. The test file's own added TODO ('add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup') concedes the gap.

[BUG] The new backup-codes assertions verify only side-effect artifacts — `download.suggestedFilename()` and a success toast — never the backup codes' content, format (XXXXX-XXXXX via formatBackupCode), or that the ten codes rendered match the ones the server generated. A regression in formatBackupCode (e.g. wrong slice indices producing 'XXXXX-XXXXX-X' garbage) or a server returning an empty/short backupCodes array passes the test, so users download unusable codes and are locked out when they lose their authenticator.

[ADVISORY] The login page's new 'lost access' toggle UI — the twoFactorLostAccess state transition, BackupCode input swap, and go-back semantics — has no test; the only e2e test file changed (login.2fa.e2e.ts) drives no backup-code login. Users who genuinely lose their authenticator — the exact scenario this feature exists for — navigate a completely untested UI path; if the toggle fails to reset form state (e.g. stale totpCode), the recovery flow breaks precisely when users have no alternative.

[BUG] Calling /setup overwrites the existing encrypted backupCodes before the user completes or even sees the new codes, so a user who confirms their password and then cancels the modal has all previously issued, unredeemed backup codes silently destroyed and replaced with codes they never viewed. A user with 2FA already enabled who opens the Enable flow (or hits the setup endpoint again) and cancels after the password step loses every backup code they saved; on next lost-access login they get MissingBackupCodes and are permanently locked out of the backup path with no way to recover their old codes.

[ADVISORY] The migration adds a nullable backupCodes column with no backfill for users who already have twoFactorEnabled=true, and the only writer is the setup endpoint which also rotates the TOTP secret, so existing 2FA users have no code path that generates backup codes without destroying and re-enrolling their authenticator. Every user who enabled 2FA before this deploy has backupCodes=null; the MissingBackupCodes error tells them to "generate them in your settings" but no settings UI/API regenerates codes independently — they must redo full TOTP setup, and if they don't, the lost-access login path is dead code for them.

[ADVISORY] The used backup code is burned (nulled and persisted) inside authorize before the session/signin completes, so any failure after this update (session cookie write failure, callback error) consumes the code without granting access. A transient failure after the prisma.user.update leaves the user with one fewer usable backup code despite never logging in; repeated partial failures can exhaust all 10 codes.

[BUG] The disable endpoint nulls backupCodes unconditionally for users authenticated via TOTP as well, but unlike the login path it performs no per-code consumption — combined with setup.ts overwriting codes on every call, there is no invariant that the codes shown at DisplayBackupCodes step are still the ones stored by the time 2FA is enabled. If the user re-opens the setup modal between enabling and the DisplayBackupCodes step (or any /setup call fires), the codes the user saved no longer match the stored set, and a later lost-access login with a saved code fails with IncorrectBackupCode.

[BUG] The copy button calls navigator.clipboard.writeText as fire-and-forget and shows the success toast unconditionally instead of on resolution. On any non-secure context or clipboard permission failure (navigator.clipboard undefined or writeText rejecting), the promise rejects with no handler and no user-visible error, yet showToast(t("backup_codes_copied"), "success") still fires — the user is told the codes were copied when the clipboard is empty and they will believe they have saved codes they never did.

[BUG] After the enable API succeeds, onEnable() is only invoked from the explicit close button; closing the dialog via ESC, the X, or onOpenChange during the DisplayBackupCodes step skips onEnable and resetState entirely. 2FA is now enabled server-side but the settings page switch state never updates and modal state (step, codes, object URL) persists — the user sees 2FA 'off' and may retry enable, a stale-state desync on a successful operation whose UI update is silently dropped.

[BUG] JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, ...)) is unguarded in the backup-code disable branch, so any decryption mismatch or non-JSON stored value throws a raw exception. A user whose backupCodes row was written with a different CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY (key rotation) or contains corrupted data gets an unhandled 500 from the disable endpoint instead of the 4xx error contract the surrounding code returns everywhere else, and the front-end falls through to generic 'something_went_wrong' with no actionable error.

[ADVISORY] The backup code is consumed (nulled and persisted) inside authorize() before the login flow has fully completed. If anything after the update throws — an adapter failure creating the session, or a concurrent-login write conflict — the code is already burned while the user is back at the login screen with one fewer working backup code and no indication it was consumed; a user retrying after a transient failure burns codes until locked out.

[ADVISORY] Each call to /setup silently overwrites the stored backupCodes with a fresh set before the user has completed enabling 2FA. A user who runs setup, records the codes shown, then abandons the flow and later re-runs setup and completes it has two sets of codes in hand; the recorded first set silently fails at login, and there is no signal that previously displayed codes were invalidated.

[ADVISORY] resetForm clears backupCode/totpCode/password but the TOTP digit inputs registered by the TwoFactor child (fields 2fa1..2fa6, plus the child's internal useState value) are never reset when toggling the lost-access branch. A user who types partial TOTP digits, hits 'lost access', submits a backup code, gets it wrong, and goes back sees a stale half-filled TOTP field state re-registered with leftover values; submission can then carry a non-empty totpCode alongside backupCode, and the server's backupCode branch masks the stale value rather than erroring — confusing retry behavior on a failed-auth path.

A user who opens the enable dialog, confirms their password, then cancels has silently had any previously issued backup codes overwritten (or new ones created) without ever viewing them — and since the login/disable paths reject a backupCode attempt only after password validation, a user who later 'loses access' and tries a code they saved from an earlier setup attempt gets `IncorrectBackupCode` with no hint that their stored list is stale.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts`, backup codes are generated (`crypto.randomBytes...`) and immediately persisted to the user row via `prisma.user.update({ data: { backupCodes: ... } })` while also setting `twoFactorEnabled: false`. The UI (`EnableTwoFactorModal.handleSetup`) calls this setup endpoint during the password-confirm step and can be canceled before 2FA is actually enabled or before backup codes are displayed (they’re only shown later at `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes`, which happens after the enable step succeeds). This means merely starting setup overwrites any existing `backupCodes` on the user record without guaranteeing the user ever saw/downloaded them, making previously saved codes stale and leading to `IncorrectBackupCode`/`MissingBackupCodes` later.

An attacker who briefly obtains a code (e.g. from a screenshot or leaked download) can reuse it concurrently with the legitimate user; single-use semantics ('Each backup code can be used exactly once') are violated.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Backup codes are generated, persisted, and returned in plaintext in the setup response before the user has confirmed anything, and a user who abandons the flow after step one ends up with stored backupCodes the user has never seen (they were never displayed since DisplayBackupCodes only runs after enable), while the enable endpoint (totp/enable.ts, untouched by this diff) has no sanity check that backupCodes still match the setup that produced the displayed QR code. A user who starts setup, sees the QR code, but closes and later re-runs setup before enabling ends up displaying/enabling against a fresh secret while stale-looking backup codes from an intermediate setup run may have been shown or downloaded — the codes shown at DisplayBackupCodes step come from the first setup response held in component state, which is correct, but a dialog closed via onOpenChange (X button) does not run resetState, so reopening the modal resumes at the stale DisplayBackupCodes step with codes from the prior user's session state rendered again.

In the UI, those codes are only displayed at `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes`, which is reached only *after* `/totp/enable` succeeds (`EnableTwoFactorModal`: on enable 200 -> `setStep(DisplayBackupCodes)`), so a user can abandon after setup (QR code step) and still have stored backup codes they were never shown in the UI. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Backup-code consumption in authorize() is a non-atomic read-modify-write: JSON.parse of the stored blob, indexOf, then a separate prisma.user.update, with no conditional WHERE on the code still being present. Two concurrent logins submitting the same backup code both pass the indexOf check (both read the pre-update blob) and both are granted a session while only one consumption is persisted — a one-time code authenticates twice; the fix requires an atomic guarded update or hashed per-code rows with a uniqueness constraint.
matched_golden_ids: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate describes the same race condition: backup codes are checked and then updated via a non-atomic read/modify/write, allowing two concurrent requests with the same code to both pass validation and authenticate, breaking one-time-use semantics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The 'no codes' sentinel is unrepresentable: MissingBackupCodes is only raised when the backupCodes column is null, but consumption writes JSON arrays of null entries, so a user who has burned all 10 codes has a non-null column of nulls. A user with zero remaining codes gets 'Backup code is incorrect' on every attempt instead of the 'missing_backup_codes' guidance ('generate them in your settings'), permanently and misleadingly — the same check exists in disable.ts and fails identically there.

adjudication.rationale: Verified in diff: backup codes are stored as an encrypted JSON array (setup.ts), and on successful backup-code login the matched entry is set to null and the array is re-encrypted (next-auth-options.ts: `backupCodes[index] = null; ... backupCodes: symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), ...)`). The only "no codes" check is `if (!user.backupCodes)` / `if (!user.backupCodes) throw MissingBackupCodes` (next-auth-options.ts) and `if (!user.backupCodes) return MissingBackupCodes` (disable.ts), which only triggers when the DB column is null/empty, not when the decrypted array contains only nulls. Once all codes are burned, `indexOf(...)` will always be -1 and the user gets IncorrectBackupCode forever instead of MissingBackupCodes guidance. The same pattern exists in disable.ts, so the finding matches the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The setup endpoint regenerates and persists a fresh backupCodes set on every invocation, and the only place the codes are ever displayed to the user is the final DisplayBackupCodes step of the enable flow. A user who confirms their password (triggering setup) and then cancels at the QR/TOTP steps has their previously-issued backup codes silently invalidated with no notice; they will later hit 'Backup code is incorrect'/'missing backup codes' with codes they carefully saved. The user-facing consequence appears at next-auth-options.ts:131.

adjudication.rationale: In `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts`, each setup call generates a new `backupCodes` array and immediately persists it to `users.backupCodes` via `prisma.user.update(...)` (along with a new encrypted `twoFactorSecret`), regardless of whether the user ever completes enabling 2FA. In `EnableTwoFactorModal`, `handleSetup` triggers this setup call at the ConfirmPassword step, but the UI does not display backup codes until *after* the enable call succeeds (it sets `step` to `DisplayBackupCodes` only on enable success). Therefore, canceling after password confirmation (during QR/TOTP steps) can silently rotate the stored backup codes without the user seeing/saving the new ones, making any previously saved codes no longer match what the server expects (as enforced in `next-auth-options.ts` backup-code verification).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Backup codes are stored reversibly encrypted (symmetricEncrypt of the plaintext codes) in a single TEXT JSON column instead of one-way hashed per-code rows, unlike one-time-code best practice. Anyone with DB read access plus the CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY (a single shared secret, no rotation) recovers all valid unused codes for every user; hashed per-code rows in a child table would also fix the consumption atomicity and the null-array sentinel problems in one shape change.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly implements backup codes as plaintext 10-char hex strings (setup.ts: `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`) and stores them reversibly encrypted in a single `users.backupCodes` TEXT column as JSON (`symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)` in `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts` and Prisma migration/schema). On login, the server decrypts the full list (`symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`) and matches the provided code, then marks a used code by setting an array element to `null` and re-encrypting (`packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts`). This means anyone with DB read access plus the shared encryption key can recover all unused backup codes for all users, which is a real security weakness introduced by this change; hashing per-code would avoid recoverability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The disable endpoint's contract now accepts both code and backupCode in one payload, and the server branch prefers backupCode whenever it is truthy, so the discrimination between 'TOTP path' and 'backup path' lives in field-emptiness rather than an explicit factor type. Any future form change that leaves a stale backupCode value in the form (e.g. a variant of resetForm that preserves it) silently routes disable through the backup-code branch and returns IncorrectBackupCode for a user who typed a valid TOTP code; the login page has the same implicit precedence in next-auth-options.ts:131, and the two client copies (Login form, DisableTwoFactorModal) of this dual-field convention will drift.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows implicit branching on truthiness of `backupCode` rather than an explicit factor type in both the disable API (`if (user.twoFactorEnabled && req.body.backupCode) ... else if (user.twoFactorEnabled) ...` in `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts`) and NextAuth authorize (`if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode) ... else if (user.twoFactorEnabled) ...` in `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts`). This means if both fields are ever present/non-empty, backup-code verification takes precedence and a valid TOTP could be ignored. Current UI attempts to clear the other field when toggling (e.g., `resetForm(false)` clears `backupCode`/`totpCode`, and login toggles clear the opposite value), so it’s not a proven bug today, but it is a concrete, diff-grounded contract/maintainability risk that could lead to subtle failures if future form/reset changes leave stale values or if clients drift.

The Dialog itself is still closable via `onOpenChange` (X/Escape/outside click depending on Dialog behavior), and there is no effect/handler in this diff that invokes `onEnable()` or even `resetState()` when the dialog is dismissed during `DisplayBackupCodes`. Therefore it’s possible for 2FA to be enabled server-side while the parent never receives onEnable, leaving parent UI (e.g., settings switch) stale.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Every call to the setup endpoint regenerates and overwrites the stored backupCodes, invalidating any codes previously issued and saved by the user. A user who runs the enable flow (or re-runs setup after a failed attempt) gets a new batch of codes each time; any codes they already downloaded/copied in a prior setup call are silently dead, directly contradicting the user-facing copy 'Each backup code can be used exactly once' and the backup-code recovery promise.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts`, the endpoint unconditionally generates a new `backupCodes` array and persists it (`backupCodes: symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), ...)`) on every call, overwriting any previously stored `user.backupCodes`. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The disable endpoint's backup-code branch accepts a backup code without consuming it (relies on the later blanket `backupCodes: null` clear), and the branch ordering means a valid backup code bypasses the TOTP check entirely while `req.body.code` is ignored. This is internally consistent for disable (codes are wiped anyway), but the asymmetry with the login path (which does consume per-code) is undocumented behavior that a future maintainer adding partial disable or backup-code reuse will trip over; the e2e TODO at apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts:12 confirms disable-with-backup-code is untested, so a regression here ships silently.

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable` now accepts `req.body.backupCode` and takes a separate branch (`if (user.twoFactorEnabled && req.body.backupCode) { ... } else if (user.twoFactorEnabled) { ... }`), so a provided backup code causes the TOTP `req.body.code` path (and its checks) to be skipped/ignored. In that backup-code branch it validates membership in the decrypted list but does not “consume” a single code; instead the handler later clears all codes unconditionally via `data: { backupCodes: null, twoFactorEnabled: false, ... }`. This is internally consistent for a full disable, but it is asymmetric with the login path in `next-auth-options.ts` where a successful backup code is explicitly removed and re-encrypted. The e2e test file also contains a TODO to add backup-code tests including disabling with backup code, so this new behavior is untested and could regress silently. This is a concrete maintainability/testing gap rather than a present functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Backup code consumption uses a read-decrypt-modify-encrypt-write sequence with no transaction or conditional update, so the same backup code can be replayed in concurrent requests. Two simultaneous logins submitting the same backup code both pass the indexOf check before either write lands (next-auth credentials callbacks run concurrently), so a single one-time code grants two sessions — defeating the single-use guarantee the copy promises ('Each backup code can be used exactly once') and letting an attacker who sniffed/copied a code use it even after the legitimate user already consumed it, if requests race.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts`, backup code verification/consumption is implemented as: decrypt `user.backupCodes` → `indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` → set `backupCodes[index] = null` → `prisma.user.update(...)` with re-encrypted array. This read-modify-write is not wrapped in a DB transaction and does not use a conditional/atomic update (e.g., update where the encrypted value/version matches or where the code is still present). With concurrent credential authorizations, two requests can both pass the `indexOf` check before either update commits, resulting in the same one-time backup code being accepted twice (two sessions created). That contradicts the stated single-use guarantee in the UI text.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Backup codes are generated with crypto.randomBytes(5).toString('hex'), yielding only 40 bits of entropy per code, well below the conventional 80+ bits for backup/recovery codes. An attacker who can submit many login attempts (e.g. via the credentials endpoint where rate limiting is per-IP and trivially distributed) has a materially better chance of guessing a valid code than against an 80-bit code; users with weak/leaked passwords get a second factor that is meaningfully brute-forceable.

adjudication.rationale: Diff explicitly generates backup codes as `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")` in `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts`, producing 10 hex chars = 40 bits of entropy per code. These codes are then accepted as an alternative to TOTP in both login (`next-auth-options.ts` checks `credentials.backupCode`) and 2FA disable (`/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts` checks `req.body.backupCode`). This makes the security strength of the backup-code second factor materially weaker than common recovery-code expectations (typically much higher than 40 bits) and is a real, diff-grounded security weakness.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Backup code verification uses backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode...) — a plain, early-exiting string comparison rather than a constant-time comparison (timingEqual/crypto.timingSafeEqual), and the same non-constant-time indexOf appears in disable.ts. Each failed attempt leaks how many leading characters of a candidate code match positions in the stored list (indexOf short-circuits per element, === per character); combined with the 40-bit code size this measurably aids online guessing by an automated attacker. Rebuttal: per-request timing jitter makes the leak impractical — but with 10 ordered codes and 40-bit values the leak compounds across attempts rather than being neutralized.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces backup-code authentication/2FA-disable paths that verify a user-supplied secret via `backupCodes.indexOf(req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` (API disable endpoint) and `backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` (NextAuth authorize). This is a normal string equality check within an array scan, not a constant-time comparison (`crypto.timingSafeEqual`), so the check is not timing-safe for an authentication secret. The finding’s claim about constant-time comparison absence and its locations is directly supported by the diff (next-auth-options.ts, disable.ts).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Every call to /setup regenerates and overwrites the stored backupCodes, silently invalidating any codes the user previously saved. A user who re-runs setup (re-scanning the QR into a new device, or any client that calls the setup endpoint) permanently voids the backup codes they already printed/stored, and they will only discover this during account recovery when every saved code returns IncorrectBackupCode — the exact lost-access scenario backup codes exist to prevent.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts`, each request generates a fresh `backupCodes` array (`crypto.randomBytes...`) and unconditionally writes it to `user.backupCodes` via `prisma.user.update({ data: { backupCodes: symmetricEncrypt(...) } })`. There is no guard for an existing `backupCodes` value or for `user.twoFactorEnabled`, so calling `/setup` again overwrites previously issued backup codes (and also resets `twoFactorEnabled` to `false`). That invalidates any codes the user previously saved, matching the finding’s core claim about regeneration/overwrite.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The missing-encryption-key branch throws new Error(ErrorCode.InternalServerError) instead of returning a res.status(500).json({error: ...}) like every other error path in the handler. An operator who misconfigures CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY gets an unhandled exception (stack trace in server logs, generic 500 HTML to the client) instead of a structured error the frontend's errorMessages map can render, turning a config problem into an opaque crash for the user disabling 2FA.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts`, the new backup-code path does `if (!process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY) { ...; throw new Error(ErrorCode.InternalServerError); }` rather than returning `res.status(...).json({ error: ... })`, while other error paths in the handler use structured JSON responses (e.g. `IncorrectPassword`, `MissingBackupCodes`, etc.). With no surrounding try/catch shown in the diff, this would surface as an unhandled exception and a non-JSON 500 response to the client, breaking the frontend’s ability to render a mapped error message for this misconfiguration case.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The disable endpoint accepts a backup code without deleting the used code from the list before success, relying entirely on the final backupCodes: null write at line 107 — and it checks the code against a list that may contain nulls from prior logins but performs no audit/logging of backup-code-based 2FA disable. Two concurrent disable requests both pass the indexOf check and both proceed (same race as the login path), and an attacker who obtains password + one backup code can disable 2FA with no security event logged for monitoring/alerting that a recovery-code-based disable occurred.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts`, the backup-code path only verifies membership (`const index = backupCodes.indexOf(...)`) and does not mutate/re-encrypt the backup-code list the way the login path does (`packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts` sets `backupCodes[index] = null` and updates). It relies on the final `prisma.user.update({ data: { backupCodes: null, twoFactorEnabled: false, ... }})` to clear all codes on success. That means there’s no explicit one-time consumption of a specific backup code in this endpoint and no event/audit logging shown for “disabled 2FA via backup code”; however, since the endpoint’s purpose is to disable 2FA and it clears `backupCodes` on success, this is more of a security/observability hardening concern than a directly verifiable functional defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The 2FA-enable e2e test uses `expect(...isChecked()).toBeTruthy()`, a false-confidence assertion that passes even when the switch is not checked, as the diff's own FIXME comment admits. The enable-2FA flow's core success state (the toggle actually switching on) is unverified; a regression that renders the switch unchecked while still returning 200 from setup/enable passes this test, and every downstream 2FA test in the file inherits the false confidence.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts` the test does `await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy();`. This asserts on the truthiness of a Promise/boolean-returning call rather than asserting the locator state itself, and the diff even adds a `// FIXME: this passes even when switch is not checked` comment directly above it. So the enable-2FA test can report success without verifying the switch is actually checked, giving false confidence and potentially masking regressions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The backup-code login branch in authorize() — including the one-time-use consumption logic (`backupCodes[index] = null` + re-encrypt) and the IncorrectBackupCode/MissingBackupCodes error paths — has zero test coverage in this diff; I checked apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts (the only test file changed), which exercises only the TOTP enable/download/copy path. The single-use invariant of backup codes is completely unverified: a bug that reuses a burned code, fails to persist the null, or throws the wrong ErrorCode ships silently, allowing replayed backup codes to grant account access. The test file's own added TODO ('add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup') concedes the gap.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new backup-code authentication logic in `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts` (`if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode) { ... backupCodes[index] = null; ... prisma.user.update(...) }`) and new error paths (`IncorrectBackupCode`, `MissingBackupCodes`). The only modified e2e test (`apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts`) explicitly contains a TODO about adding backup-code tests and currently exercises only the TOTP enable flow plus backup-code *display/download/copy UI*—not login via backup code nor the one-time-use persistence/consumption invariant. That’s a concrete, diff-grounded gap in coverage for newly added security-sensitive behavior, but it’s not a directly verifiable defect in the implementation itself from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new backup-codes assertions verify only side-effect artifacts — `download.suggestedFilename()` and a success toast — never the backup codes' content, format (XXXXX-XXXXX via formatBackupCode), or that the ten codes rendered match the ones the server generated. A regression in formatBackupCode (e.g. wrong slice indices producing 'XXXXX-XXXXX-X' garbage) or a server returning an empty/short backupCodes array passes the test, so users download unusable codes and are locked out when they lose their authenticator.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts`, the newly added backup-code checks only assert the download filename (`download.suggestedFilename()`), the presence of a success toast after copy (`toast-success`), and closing the dialog. The diff even includes `// TODO: check file content` and `// TODO: check clipboard content`, and there is no assertion that the rendered `backupCodes` list has length 10 or that `formatBackupCode` produced `XXXXX-XXXXX`. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test coverage gap for newly added backup-code generation/formatting logic, not a product defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The login page's new 'lost access' toggle UI — the twoFactorLostAccess state transition, BackupCode input swap, and go-back semantics — has no test; the only e2e test file changed (login.2fa.e2e.ts) drives no backup-code login. Users who genuinely lose their authenticator — the exact scenario this feature exists for — navigate a completely untested UI path; if the toggle fails to reset form state (e.g. stale totpCode), the recovery flow breaks precisely when users have no alternative.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new login recovery path gated by `twoFactorLostAccess` in `apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx`, swapping `<TwoFactor>` for `<BackupCode>` and adding a new "Lost access" button plus altered go-back behavior (clearing either `totpCode` or `backupCode`). The only touched e2e test (`apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts`) explicitly contains a TODO for backup-code tests and does not exercise backup-code login or the toggle/go-back semantics. This is a specific, diff-grounded coverage gap for newly added nontrivial UI state logic, not a proven functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Calling /setup overwrites the existing encrypted backupCodes before the user completes or even sees the new codes, so a user who confirms their password and then cancels the modal has all previously issued, unredeemed backup codes silently destroyed and replaced with codes they never viewed. A user with 2FA already enabled who opens the Enable flow (or hits the setup endpoint again) and cancels after the password step loses every backup code they saved; on next lost-access login they get MissingBackupCodes and are permanently locked out of the backup path with no way to recover their old codes.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts`, the `/setup` handler now generates `backupCodes` and immediately persists them via `prisma.user.update({ data: { backupCodes: symmetricEncrypt(...), twoFactorEnabled: false, twoFactorSecret: ... } })` before the user finishes enabling 2FA or confirms they saved the codes. The UI flow (`EnableTwoFactorModal.handleSetup`) calls this endpoint right after password confirmation; if the user cancels the modal after that, the DB has already had any existing `user.backupCodes` overwritten with new codes the user may never have seen/saved. This is silent data loss of previously issued backup codes. (The finding’s mention of `MissingBackupCodes` specifically is not guaranteed by the diff—after overwrite the codes are still present—but the destructive overwrite behavior is real.)

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The migration adds a nullable backupCodes column with no backfill for users who already have twoFactorEnabled=true, and the only writer is the setup endpoint which also rotates the TOTP secret, so existing 2FA users have no code path that generates backup codes without destroying and re-enrolling their authenticator. Every user who enabled 2FA before this deploy has backupCodes=null; the MissingBackupCodes error tells them to "generate them in your settings" but no settings UI/API regenerates codes independently — they must redo full TOTP setup, and if they don't, the lost-access login path is dead code for them.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a nullable `users.backupCodes` column (migration + Prisma schema) but does not backfill it for existing users with `twoFactorEnabled=true`. The only code path that writes `backupCodes` is the TOTP setup endpoint (`/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts`), which also generates a new TOTP secret and stores it (i.e., re-enrollment). Meanwhile, the new “Lost access” flows in login (`pages/auth/login.tsx` + `next-auth-options.ts`) and disable 2FA (`totp/disable.ts` + `DisableTwoFactorModal`) require `user.backupCodes` and explicitly error with `MissingBackupCodes` when null. There is no independent UI/API in the diff to generate/regenerate backup codes without going through full setup, so for pre-existing 2FA users the new lost-access path is effectively unusable (always hits MissingBackupCodes) unless they redo setup and rotate their authenticator secret.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The used backup code is burned (nulled and persisted) inside authorize before the session/signin completes, so any failure after this update (session cookie write failure, callback error) consumes the code without granting access. A transient failure after the prisma.user.update leaves the user with one fewer usable backup code despite never logging in; repeated partial failures can exhaust all 10 codes.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts`, the backup code is invalidated and persisted (`backupCodes[index] = null; await prisma.user.update(...)`) inside `authorize` immediately after verification, before NextAuth completes the sign-in flow (session/JWT creation, cookie write, callbacks). Since `authorize` runs prior to those later steps, any failure after this DB update (e.g., callback error, session/cookie write failure) would consume a backup code without successfully logging the user in, permanently reducing usable codes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The disable endpoint nulls backupCodes unconditionally for users authenticated via TOTP as well, but unlike the login path it performs no per-code consumption — combined with setup.ts overwriting codes on every call, there is no invariant that the codes shown at DisplayBackupCodes step are still the ones stored by the time 2FA is enabled. If the user re-opens the setup modal between enabling and the DisplayBackupCodes step (or any /setup call fires), the codes the user saved no longer match the stored set, and a later lost-access login with a saved code fails with IncorrectBackupCode.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts` generates and stores `backupCodes` and also sets `twoFactorEnabled: false` every time it is called. That means any subsequent `/setup` call would actually disable 2FA (and rotate `twoFactorSecret`) rather than silently leaving 2FA enabled while only changing the backup-code set. Therefore the finding’s claimed state—2FA enabled but backup codes silently overwritten so that later “lost-access” backup login fails—is not supported by the diff. Additionally, the disable endpoint clearing `backupCodes: null` unconditionally is consistent with disabling 2FA and makes per-code consumption irrelevant there.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The copy button calls navigator.clipboard.writeText as fire-and-forget and shows the success toast unconditionally instead of on resolution. On any non-secure context or clipboard permission failure (navigator.clipboard undefined or writeText rejecting), the promise rejects with no handler and no user-visible error, yet showToast(t("backup_codes_copied"), "success") still fires — the user is told the codes were copied when the clipboard is empty and they will believe they have saved codes they never did.

adjudication.rationale: In `EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx`, the DisplayBackupCodes copy button handler calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` without `await`/`.then`/`.catch` and immediately calls `showToast(t("backup_codes_copied"), "success")` unconditionally. This can both (a) produce an unhandled rejected promise if clipboard access fails/denied or `navigator.clipboard` is unavailable, and (b) mislead the user with a success toast even when nothing was copied. This behavior is directly shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] After the enable API succeeds, onEnable() is only invoked from the explicit close button; closing the dialog via ESC, the X, or onOpenChange during the DisplayBackupCodes step skips onEnable and resetState entirely. 2FA is now enabled server-side but the settings page switch state never updates and modal state (step, codes, object URL) persists — the user sees 2FA 'off' and may retry enable, a stale-state desync on a successful operation whose UI update is silently dropped.

adjudication.rationale: In EnableTwoFactorModal, a successful enable now does `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)` and no longer calls `onEnable()` immediately (handleEnable success path). During `DisplayBackupCodes`, the only place that calls both `resetState()` and `onEnable()` is the explicit “close” button handler (`data-testid="backup-codes-close"`). The Dialog itself is controlled by `open`/`onOpenChange` (`<Dialog open={open} onOpenChange={onOpenChange}>`), but there is no wrapper around `onOpenChange` to invoke `resetState()`/`onEnable()` when the dialog is dismissed via ESC/X/backdrop (i.e., non-button close). Also, the Cancel button is hidden in `DisplayBackupCodes` (`step !== SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes ? <Button ...>cancel</Button> : null`). Therefore, closing the dialog through onOpenChange during the backup codes step can skip both resetState and the parent update via onEnable, leaving UI state potentially stale despite server-side enable succeeding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, ...)) is unguarded in the backup-code disable branch, so any decryption mismatch or non-JSON stored value throws a raw exception. A user whose backupCodes row was written with a different CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY (key rotation) or contains corrupted data gets an unhandled 500 from the disable endpoint instead of the 4xx error contract the surrounding code returns everywhere else, and the front-end falls through to generic 'something_went_wrong' with no actionable error.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts`, the new backup-code path does `const backupCodes = JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY));` without any guarding/try-catch. If `symmetricDecrypt(...)` throws (wrong/rotated `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, corrupted ciphertext) or the decrypted plaintext is not valid JSON, `JSON.parse` will throw and the request will fail via an unhandled exception rather than returning the endpoint’s usual structured 4xx `{ error: ErrorCode.* }` responses shown elsewhere in the handler.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The backup code is consumed (nulled and persisted) inside authorize() before the login flow has fully completed. If anything after the update throws — an adapter failure creating the session, or a concurrent-login write conflict — the code is already burned while the user is back at the login screen with one fewer working backup code and no indication it was consumed; a user retrying after a transient failure burns codes until locked out.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts`, the backup code branch verifies the code and then immediately persists consumption by updating `user.backupCodes` (sets `backupCodes[index] = null` and `await prisma.user.update(...)`) inside `authorize()` before the overall NextAuth login flow has completed. If anything after `authorize()` fails (session/token creation, adapter write, etc.), the user can end up not logged in while the backup code has already been burned, matching the finding’s concern about losing codes on transient failures.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Each call to /setup silently overwrites the stored backupCodes with a fresh set before the user has completed enabling 2FA. A user who runs setup, records the codes shown, then abandons the flow and later re-runs setup and completes it has two sets of codes in hand; the recorded first set silently fails at login, and there is no signal that previously displayed codes were invalidated.

adjudication.rationale: In `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts`, every successful setup call generates a new `backupCodes` array and immediately persists it (`backupCodes: symmetricEncrypt(...)`) to the user record before 2FA is actually enabled. This means repeating setup will overwrite previously stored backup codes (and the client also receives the new codes in the response). There’s no indication/guard in the diff that prevents or signals this invalidation if the flow is abandoned and re-run.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] resetForm clears backupCode/totpCode/password but the TOTP digit inputs registered by the TwoFactor child (fields 2fa1..2fa6, plus the child's internal useState value) are never reset when toggling the lost-access branch. A user who types partial TOTP digits, hits 'lost access', submits a backup code, gets it wrong, and goes back sees a stale half-filled TOTP field state re-registered with leftover values; submission can then carry a non-empty totpCode alongside backupCode, and the server's backupCode branch masks the stale value rather than erroring — confusing retry behavior on a failed-auth path.

adjudication.rationale: In DisableTwoFactorModal, resetForm() only clears form values for "totpCode"/"backupCode"/"password" (form.setValue(...)), but the TwoFactor component registers six separate digit fields (name={`2fa${index+1}`} with {...digit}) and maintains its own local state. When toggling `twoFactorLostAccess`, TwoFactor unmounts/remounts; with react-hook-form's default behavior (values retained when fields unmount unless explicitly unregistered/reset), the 2fa1..2fa6 values are not cleared by resetForm, so they can reappear as stale partially-filled inputs when switching back from BackupCode. This can also re-populate/affect the derived totpCode depending on TwoFactor's wiring, creating confusing retry behavior. The diff shows the clearing logic omission and the toggle path that triggers it (resetForm(false) on the lost_access button).
